children: Extremely dry weather is disrupting coal shipments from a number of miners in Indonesia's Kalimantan as river water levels recede, an industry group said on Wednesday.

Indonesia, the world's largest thermal coal exporter, is experiencing "super-El Niño" weather conditions which have caused drought and exacerbated wildfires in Sumatra and Kalimantan, home of many of the country's coal mines.

Local media reported that the water levels of the Mahakam River, a key logistic route which stretches 980 kilometres (608.94 miles), have been receding in recent weeks. Data from Indonesia's weather agency showed that there was almost no precipitation in East Kalimantan for the whole of August.

Some members of the Indonesia Coal Miners Association in East Kalimantan on Borneo island have reported difficulties in transportation due to the river's low water levels, the group's executive director Gita Mahyarani told Reuters.
She said those members have been forced to limit the volume of coal loaded onto barges to prevent grounding.

"Consequently, the carrying capacity per trip decreases, trip frequency rises, and logistic costs increase," Gita said, adding that the extent of the impact varies by company, depending on the location of their mines and the specific sections of the waterway they need to navigate.
The group does not have an estimate of how much volume has been affected by the condition of the river.
Barges that could typically carry 7,000 metric tons were forced to lower their load to around 5,500 tons, local port authority official Mursidi told the Kompas news website on Wednesday.
He added that despite reducing their load, some barges still faced difficulties travelling upstream due to the lower water levels.
